title: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
summary: How a transformer reranker reads a query and passage in one sequence, why its scores cannot be precomputed, how logits become scores, how it is trained with hard negatives, and what 100 candidates cost.
outcomes: Explain why joint attention makes cross-encoders more accurate and why their scores cannot be precomputed
Compute the document token budget for a query-passage pair under max_length 512 truncation
Convert reranker logits to sigmoid scores and explain why the ranking does not change
Compare pointwise, pairwise and listwise losses and explain why hard negatives matter
Estimate rerank latency for k candidates from throughput and explain Margin-MSE distillation

lessons.title: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together

blocks.md:
The multi-stage retrieval course left you with a pipeline: a cheap first stage (BM25, dense, or hybrid) returns a few hundred candidates, and a slower second stage reorders them. This course is about the model that usually sits in that second stage: the **cross-encoder reranker**.

A **cross-encoder** is a transformer that takes the query and one candidate document as a single input sequence and outputs one number, a relevance score. It produces no embedding. To rank 100 candidates it runs 100 forward passes, one per (query, document) pair.

Compare that with the **bi-encoder** you met in dense retrieval. A bi-encoder encodes the query and each document *separately* into vectors and scores them with a dot product or cosine. Because a document vector never depends on the query, you can compute every document vector once, offline, and put them in an index.

That independence is also the bi-encoder's weakness: the whole document must be squeezed into one fixed vector before the model knows what will be asked about it.

scenes.caption: Bi-encoder: query and document go through the encoder separately. The two only meet at the very end, in a single dot product.
The document path does not depend on the query, so it runs offline once per document and the vectors are stored in an index. At query time only the query is encoded.
Cross-encoder: the query and the document are packed into one sequence. Every layer lets query tokens and document tokens attend to each other.
The output is one score, not a vector. Nothing about the document can be reused for the next query, so the whole transformer runs once per pair.

blocks.md:
Why is reading both together more accurate? In a cross-encoder, the representation of each document token is computed *while looking at the query*. The model can check whether the passage actually answers the question, whether a matching word is used in the same sense, and whether a negation flips the meaning. A bi-encoder can only compare two summaries.

The Sentence Transformers documentation states the trade-off directly: cross-encoders achieve better performance than bi-encoders but do not produce an embedding, so they cannot be indexed and are applied to a short candidate list instead.

The idea entered mainstream retrieval with **monoBERT** (Nogueira and Cho, 2019). They fine-tuned BERT-large as a binary relevance classifier and reranked the top 1,000 BM25 results on the MS MARCO passage task. On the MS MARCO eval set, MRR@10 went from 16.5 for untuned BM25 to 35.8 with BERT-large reranking, the top of the leaderboard at the time.

**MS MARCO passage ranking** is a dataset of about 8.8 million passages and real Bing queries, with on average one passage labeled relevant per query. **MRR@10** is the mean, over queries, of 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result, counting 0 when none appears in the top 10.

A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

blocks.question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

blocks.question: Which statement about what a cross-encoder outputs is correct?
options: A query embedding and a document embedding that are compared with cosine
A ranked list of document ids from its own index
One relevance score per (query, document) pair
A probability distribution over the whole vocabulary for each document token
blocks.explain: A reranker such as monoBERT or bge-reranker returns a single number per pair. Ranking comes from sorting candidates by that number; there is no embedding and no index inside the model.

lessons.title: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit

blocks.md:
Before the transformer runs, the tokenizer turns the (query, document) pair into one sequence. For a BERT-style model the layout is `[CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP]`. The **[CLS]** token is a special first token whose final hidden state will be used to produce the score. Each **[SEP]** marks the end of a segment.

BERT also adds **segment ids** (in Hugging Face, `token_type_ids`): 0 for `[CLS]`, the query and the first `[SEP]`, and 1 for the document and the final `[SEP]`. These, added to the token and position embeddings, tell the model which side each token came from.

Our running example: the query `cheap flights to paris from new york in june` tokenizes to 9 wordpieces with the bert-base-uncased tokenizer, and a candidate article is 700 tokens long. The model was trained with **max_length** 512: position embeddings exist only for 512 positions, so the packed sequence cannot be longer.

With three special tokens, the room left for the document is $512 - 9 - 3 = 500$ tokens. The last 200 document tokens are simply cut off.

blocks.title: How a 700-token document is packed into 512 positions

scenes.caption: The raw pair would be 1 + 9 + 1 + 700 + 1 = 712 tokens. Cells are grouped: doc1 is document tokens 1 to 100, doc2 is 101 to 200, and so on.
Segment ids: 0 for the [CLS], query and first [SEP]; 1 for the document and the final [SEP]. Only BERT-style models use them; XLM-RoBERTa models do not.
max_length 512 leaves 500 document tokens. Truncation removes doc6 and doc7 (tokens 501 to 700); the final [SEP] is still added after the cut.
Anything relevant in the last 200 tokens is invisible to the reranker. It scores the first 500 document tokens only.

blocks.code:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
enc = tok("cheap flights to paris from new york in june",  # sentence A
          long_article_text,       # sentence B: the document
          truncation="only_second",  # cut the document, never the query
          max_length=512)
print(len(enc["input_ids"]))       # 512
print(set(enc["token_type_ids"]))  # {0, 1}
blocks.caption: Passing the query and document as two arguments makes the tokenizer insert [CLS] and [SEP] and the segment ids for you. long_article_text is a placeholder for the 700-token text.

blocks.md:
Which side gets cut? The Hugging Face tokenizer's `truncation=True` means the **longest_first** strategy: it removes tokens one at a time from whichever sequence of the pair is currently longer. With a short query and a long passage that is the passage, so the result matches `only_second` here. `only_second` makes the intent explicit.

monoBERT went further and capped the query itself at 64 tokens, then truncated the passage so the full concatenation fit in 512. XLM-RoBERTa models, which several BGE rerankers are built on, pack a pair as `<s> A </s></s> B </s>`: four special tokens and no segment ids, so a 9-token query leaves 499 document tokens.

blocks.prompt: A support article has the answer in its last paragraph, around token 650. The same query is used with a reranker at max_length 512. What happens to that article's score?
blocks.reveal:
The reranker never sees the answer. It scores only the first 500 document tokens, so a document can be ranked low even though it is the best answer.

monoT5 handled long documents (TREC Robust04, about 460 words on average) by splitting each document into passages with a sliding window of 10 sentences and stride 5, scoring each passage, and taking the **maximum** passage score as the document score.

blocks.md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

Check what fraction of your candidates actually exceed max_length. monoT5's authors note that with 512 input tokens none of the MS MARCO passages needed truncation, while full web documents almost always do.

blocks.question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
blocks.explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

blocks.question: You switch from a BERT-based reranker to an XLM-RoBERTa-based one and keep the same max_length. Which detail changes in packing?
options: The query is now placed after the document
There are no special tokens at all
The model accepts 1,024 positions automatically
The pair uses four special tokens and no segment ids, so one fewer document token fits
blocks.explain: XLM-RoBERTa packs a pair as <s> A </s></s> B </s> and does not use token type ids. Order and the max_length you pass stay the same; the budget for the document shrinks by one token.

lessons.title: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other

blocks.md:
Recall from the attention course: each token builds a query vector and a key vector, scores every other token by a scaled dot product, and softmaxes the scores into weights that sum to 1. In a cross-encoder the sequence contains both texts, so this happens over **all** query and document tokens together, in every layer.

To see what that buys, here is a toy single attention head over our packed pair `[CLS] cheap flights [SEP] low cost airfare paris [SEP]`.

Simplified model: each token gets a hand-made 4-dimensional vector (dimensions roughly meaning price, travel, place, special token) and we use it as both query and key, so the weight from token $i$ to token $j$ is $\mathrm{softmax}_j(e_i \cdot e_j / \sqrt{4})$. Real models learn separate query and key projections and have many heads and layers. The numbers below were computed with a script.

blocks.title: Toy attention weights over the packed pair

scenes.caption: Full attention matrix. Row i shows how token i spreads its attention; each row sums to 1. Query tokens are the cheap and flights rows; document tokens are the low, cost, airfare and paris rows.
Query rows looking at document columns. cheap puts 0.21 on low and 0.17 on cost; flights puts 0.29 on airfare. About half of each query token's attention lands on the document.
It also runs the other way: the document token low puts 0.27 on cheap, more than on itself (0.20). Its next-layer state now carries information about this specific query.
Bi-encoder pattern: block the cross-segment cells and renormalize. Now low spreads 0.35, 0.30, 0.16 over document tokens only, and cheap mostly attends to itself (0.71).

blocks.md:
The last scene is the key point. In the bi-encoder, the row for `low` is the same whatever the query is, so its output can be cached. In the cross-encoder, `low` attends to `cheap` with weight 0.27, so its hidden state after this layer depends on the query. Every later layer builds on those query-dependent states.

That is why cross-encoder scores **cannot be precomputed**: there is no query-independent intermediate result to store, except the token embeddings at the very input.
Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

Now the cost. For a packed length $n = q + d$, each attention head in each layer forms an $n \times n$ score matrix, so the attention part grows as $O((q+d)^2)$. The rest of the layer (the query, key, value and output projections plus the feed-forward block) grows linearly in $n$.

Kaplan et al. give a standard count for forward-pass compute per token, where $N$ is the number of non-embedding parameters and $n_{layer}$, $d_{model}$ are depth and width:

blocks.tex: C_{\text{forward}} \approx 2N + 2\, n_{layer}\, n\, d_{model} \quad\text{FLOPs per token}, \qquad N = 12\, n_{layer}\, d_{model}^2
blocks.caption: Multiply by n tokens for one pair. The first term is the linear layers; the second is Kaplan's attention term (labeled "Attention: Mask", the QK scores), which is why the total has an n squared part. Bidirectional QK plus value mixing is about twice this.

blocks.md: Plug in BERT-base: $n_{layer} = 12$, $d_{model} = 768$, so $N \approx 84.9$ million non-embedding parameters (BERT-base has 110M in total including embeddings). One pair at 512 tokens costs about 91.8 GFLOP, of which only 4.83 GFLOP (5.3 percent) is Kaplan's quadratic attention term. Counting both the score and the value-mixing products of bidirectional attention doubles it to about 9.7 GFLOP, roughly 10 percent: still a small share.

blocks.title: Forward GFLOP for one pair, BERT-base

scenes.caption: Total forward compute per pair from the formula above: 5.5, 22.0, 44.7 and 91.8 GFLOP. Doubling n from 256 to 512 multiplies it by 2.05.
Only the attention term, which grows with n squared: 0.02, 0.3, 1.21 and 4.83 GFLOP. It quadruples per doubling but is still small at 512 for a model this wide.

blocks.prompt: You halve max_length from 512 to 256 for a BERT-base reranker on passages long enough to fill either limit. Roughly how much compute per pair do you save?
blocks.reveal: About half, not three quarters. The total drops from 91.8 to 44.7 GFLOP, a factor of 2.05. The $(q+d)^2$ attention term does shrink by 4x, but at these lengths it is only about 5 to 10 percent of the work, depending on how you count it; the linear layers dominate. The quadratic term matters more for much longer inputs or narrower models.

blocks.md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

blocks.question: Why can a search engine cache document embeddings for a bi-encoder but not intermediate document states for a cross-encoder?
options: Cross-encoder hidden states are too large to store
In a cross-encoder every document token attends to the query tokens in every layer, so its states differ for each query
Cross-encoders use random dropout at inference time
Bi-encoders use a different tokenizer that is deterministic
blocks.explain: Attention mixes query tokens into each document token's representation from the first layer on. A cache keyed by document would be wrong for every new query. Size is a secondary issue; dropout is off at inference.

blocks.question: Using the course's formula, one BERT-base pair at 256 tokens costs about 44.7 GFLOP. Roughly how much compute does reranking 100 such candidates take, compared with encoding a 32-token query once with a bi-encoder of the same size (5.45 GFLOP)?
options: About the same
About 10 times more
About 800 times more
About 100,000 times more
blocks.explain: 100 x 44.7 GFLOP is about 4.47 TFLOP, versus 5.45 GFLOP for the query encoding: a ratio of roughly 820. The 100 dot products against cached document vectors add only about 0.15 MFLOP.

lessons.title: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token

blocks.md:
After the last layer, the model reads the final hidden state of `[CLS]`, a vector $h$ (768 numbers in BERT-base), and applies a single linear layer. The result is one unnormalized number, the **logit** $z$. Applying the **sigmoid** $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ maps it into the range 0 to 1, which training treats as the probability that the passage is relevant.

monoBERT describes exactly this: the [CLS] vector feeds a single-layer network that outputs the probability of relevance, computed for each passage independently, and the candidates are sorted by it.

blocks.tex: z = w^\top h_{[CLS]} + b, \qquad s = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
blocks.caption: w and b are the only new parameters added on top of the pretrained transformer; everything is fine-tuned together.

blocks.md:
Real outputs from the documentation of two popular rerankers:

- Sentence Transformers' `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2` returns logits 8.607 for a Berlin population passage and -4.320 for a passage about Berlin museums. Sigmoid maps them to 0.9998 and 0.0131.
- The `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` model card shows a raw score of -5.652 for a toy pair and 0.0035 with `normalize=True`, which applies sigmoid.

Sigmoid is monotonic, so it never changes the order of candidates. The Sentence Transformers docs say so explicitly: MS MARCO models return logits, and adding a Sigmoid activation gives 0 to 1 scores without changing the ranking. Use sigmoid when you need a threshold or a comparable confidence, not to improve ranking.
Here is a worked rerank. The first stage returned five candidates P1 to P5 in that order. The cross-encoder produced the logits below (illustrative values), and we convert and sort.

blocks.title: Reranking five candidates
blocks.code:
cands = ["P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P5"]  # first-stage order
logits = model.predict([(query, text[c]) for c in cands])
probs = [sigmoid(z) for z in logits]
ranked = sorted(zip(cands, probs), key=lambda t: -t[1])
return ranked[:3]

scenes.caption: The first stage hands over five candidates in its own order.
One forward pass per pair, batched together. Each returns a raw logit.
Sigmoid maps logits into 0 to 1. Notice 4.3 and 7.9 both look like near certainty after the squash.
Sort by score. P5, last in the first stage, becomes first. Sorting by logits would give the same order.
Return the top 3 to the user or to an LLM as context.

blocks.title: Logit versus sigmoid score for the five candidates

scenes.caption: Raw logits. They are unbounded and can be negative; only the order and differences are meaningful.
After sigmoid. The order is identical, but the 3.6 logit gap between P5 and P2 shrinks to 0.013, which is why thresholds near 1 behave badly.

blocks.md:
**monoT5** (Nogueira, Jiang and Lin, 2020) reaches the same kind of score with an encoder-decoder model. The input is the text `Query: q Document: d Relevant:` and T5 is fine-tuned to generate the word `true` or `false`.

At inference it runs one decoding step and applies a softmax over only the two logits for `true` and `false`, then ranks by the probability of `true`. The authors report that ranking by the raw `true` logit, or by a softmax over the whole vocabulary, gave metrics close to zero.

blocks.caption: A two-way softmax is a sigmoid of the logit difference. With z_true = 3.1 and z_false = -1.4, p(true) = sigma(4.5) = 0.989.

blocks.md: On the MS MARCO passage dev set, reranking BM25's top 1,000, monoT5 reported MRR@10 of 0.363 (T5-base), 0.383 (T5-large) and 0.382 (T5-3B) against 0.372 for BERT-large. Its clearer advantage was data efficiency: trained on only 2,000 examples, T5-base reached 0.238 MRR@10 while BERT-base reached 0.127, below the BM25 baseline of 0.184.

blocks.question: Your service returns reranker scores to a client that drops every result with score below 0.5. You switch from logits to sigmoid outputs. What changes?
options: The ranking order changes for many queries
Nothing at all
The order stays the same, but now the 0.5 threshold corresponds to logit 0, so the filter keeps different results than before
Sigmoid makes the scores calibrated probabilities across all queries
blocks.explain: Sigmoid is monotonic, so order is unchanged, but a fixed threshold now cuts at logit 0 instead of at 0.5 logits. Sigmoid outputs are not automatically calibrated; whether 0.7 really means 70 percent relevant depends on training data and should be checked.

blocks.question: In monoT5, why does ranking by the softmax over all vocabulary tokens work poorly compared with the two-token softmax?
options: Because the vocabulary softmax is too slow to compute
Because probability mass on thousands of unrelated tokens varies across inputs and swamps the true versus false comparison
Because T5 cannot output the word true
Because the vocabulary softmax is not differentiable
blocks.explain: The paper reports near-zero metrics for that variant. Restricting to the two target tokens turns the output into a clean binary decision, sigma(z_true minus z_false), that is comparable across candidates.

lessons.title: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives

blocks.md:
Training data for a reranker is a set of queries, each with at least one relevant passage (a **positive**) and some non-relevant passages (**negatives**). How you turn those into a loss, and which negatives you pick, changes what the model learns.

Our worked group: one query with a positive scored $z = 2.0$, an **easy negative** (a random passage, $z = -4.0$) and two **hard negatives** ($z = 1.5$ and $0.5$). A hard negative is a passage that looks relevant, typically one ranked high by the first-stage retriever, but is not.
**Pointwise** loss treats each pair as an independent binary classification. monoBERT used exactly this cross-entropy, with negatives drawn from BM25's top 1,000:

blocks.tex: L_{\text{point}} = -\sum_{j \in J_{pos}} \log s_j \; - \sum_{j \in J_{neg}} \log(1 - s_j), \qquad s_j = \sigma(z_j)
blocks.caption: Binary cross-entropy (BCE). The gradient with respect to the logit is s_j minus the label.

blocks.title: Loss per candidate under each objective

scenes.caption: Pointwise BCE per item: 0.127, 0.018, 1.701, 0.974 (mean 0.705). The easy negative contributes almost nothing; its gradient is only 0.018.
Pairwise (RankNet-style) loss per pair, log(1 + e^(z_neg - z_pos)), against the positive: 0.002, 0.474, 0.201 (mean 0.226). Only relative order matters now.
Listwise softmax over the whole group: probabilities 0.546, 0.001, 0.331, 0.122. The loss is -log 0.546 = 0.605, and the hard negatives take almost all the probability the positive lacks.

blocks.md:
**Pairwise** losses compare a positive with a negative and penalize the model when the negative scores close to or above the positive, regardless of absolute values. Hofstatter et al. trained their BERT_CAT teachers with this kind of RankNet loss.

**Listwise** losses look at a whole group at once. Gao, Dai and Callan's **Localized Contrastive Estimation (LCE)** softmaxes the scores of one positive and $n$ negatives from the same query, and the negatives are *localized*: sampled from the top $m$ results of the very retriever the reranker will sit behind.

blocks.caption: G_q holds the positive and the sampled negatives for query q; z is the [CLS] projection score.

blocks.prompt: Replace the two hard negatives in our group with two more random passages scored -3.5 and -5.0. What happens to the LCE loss, and what does that mean for learning?
blocks.reveal: It collapses from 0.605 to 0.0074. With only easy negatives the positive already wins by a huge margin, so the gradient is near zero and the model learns almost nothing. Rerankers only ever see the top of a retriever's list, where every candidate looks plausible, so training must contain negatives of that kind.

blocks.md:
Gao et al. found that a reranker trained the vanilla way (pointwise BCE) did not fully benefit when the first stage got better, because better retrievers return harder false positives. With LCE and negatives sampled from the target retriever's top 100, MRR@100 on MS MARCO document dev rose in all four pipelines they tested, for example from 40.84 to 43.38 behind the HDCT retriever.

Sentence Transformers exposes the same building blocks: `BinaryCrossEntropyLoss` (pointwise, on logits), `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss` (an InfoNCE-style softmax over a positive and negatives), learning-to-rank losses such as `LambdaLoss` and `ListNetLoss`, and `mine_hard_negatives` to collect hard negatives with an embedding model.

The Sentence Transformers loss overview still calls BinaryCrossEntropyLoss very hard to outperform for labeled pairs. The bigger lever is usually the negatives: mine them from the retriever you will deploy behind, and filter out ones scored almost as high as the positive, since some will be unlabeled positives.

Hard negative mining has a trap: MS MARCO labels about one relevant passage per query, so many top-ranked unlabeled passages are actually relevant. Training to push them down teaches the model wrong lessons. mine_hard_negatives offers margins and a max_score cap partly to skip such false negatives.

blocks.question: A reranker trained with random negatives scores 0.95 on a held-out set of (positive, random negative) pairs but barely beats BM25 when deployed behind a strong dense retriever. What is the most likely cause?
options: The training negatives were easy, so the model never learned to separate the plausible near-misses it sees in deployment
The learning rate was too low
Sigmoid outputs should have been used instead of logits
max_length was set to 512 instead of 1,024
blocks.explain: This is the failure LCE addresses. Random negatives are separable by surface cues, so the evaluation looks great while the deployed candidate lists contain only plausible passages. Mine negatives from the target retriever's top results.

blocks.question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
blocks.explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

lessons.title: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation

blocks.md:
Because every candidate costs a full forward pass, reranker latency is roughly linear in the number of candidates $k$. A simple model: if a GPU sustains a throughput of $T$ pairs per second at your passage length, scoring $k$ candidates takes about $1000\,k / T$ milliseconds, plus fixed overhead for tokenization and transfer.

The Sentence Transformers model card for the MS MARCO cross-encoders lists measured throughput on a V100 GPU: about 9,000 docs/sec for TinyBERT-L2-v2, 1,800 for MiniLM-L6-v2, 960 for MiniLM-L12-v2 and 100 for a BERT-large reranker.

blocks.title: Rerank latency versus number of candidates

scenes.caption: MiniLM-L6-v2 at 1,800 pairs/s: 100 candidates take 1000 x 100 / 1800 = 55.6 ms, and 1,000 candidates 555.6 ms. Simplified: assumes throughput holds at every batch size.
MiniLM-L12-v2 at 960 pairs/s: 104.2 ms for 100 candidates. Its listed MRR@10 is 39.02 versus 39.01 for L6, so here the extra layers buy almost nothing.
TinyBERT-L2-v2 at 9,000 pairs/s: 11.1 ms for 100. Its listed MRR@10 drops to 32.56. Each throughput comes with its own accuracy.
A BERT-large reranker at 100 pairs/s needs 1,000 ms for 100 candidates. Deep rerank lists and large models do not fit an interactive budget on one GPU.

blocks.md: A second, independent measurement agrees on the order of magnitude. Hofstatter et al. timed 1 query against 1,000 passages on a TITAN RTX GPU and report a median of 950 ms for a DistilBERT cross-encoder (BERT_CAT), against 23 ms for a DistilBERT dot-product model with cached passage vectors. That is about 95 ms per 100 candidates.

blocks.title: Where the time goes for one query

scenes.caption: Assumed: 8 ms first stage, 2 ms to tokenize, then MiniLM-L6-v2 at 1,800 pairs/s in batches of 32. 100 candidates finish at about 65.6 ms.
Split the 100 pairs across two GPUs (50 each). Model time halves and the query finishes at about 37.8 ms. Throughput, not the model, is what you scale.
Or rerank only the top 30: one batch, done at about 26.7 ms. The cost is recall: a relevant passage at first-stage rank 40 can no longer be promoted.

blocks.md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

The other way to use a cross-encoder's accuracy is **distillation**: train a fast bi-encoder to imitate it. Hofstatter et al. proposed **Margin-MSE**. A trained cross-encoder teacher $M_t$ scores training triples (query, relevant passage, non-relevant passage) once, offline. The student $M_s$ is trained so that its *margin*, the score difference between the two passages, matches the teacher's margin.

blocks.caption: Only the difference is matched, so the student may use any score range.

scenes.caption: Step 1, offline: the trained cross-encoder scores every triple once (illustrative scores 9.1 and 2.3). The scores are stored and reused.
Step 2: the bi-encoder student scores the same triple with dot products (31.2 and 27.0). Its scale is very different from the teacher's.
Only margins are compared: (4.2 - 6.8) squared = 6.76. Matching raw scores would give a meaningless 549.25 here because the scales differ.

blocks.md: Distillation lets the expensive model's judgments improve the cheap first stage, which then hands the reranker better candidates. Hofstatter et al. found Margin-MSE beat pointwise MSE and weighted RankNet as a distillation loss for each student architecture they tested, and an ensemble of teachers helped further in most cases. Sentence Transformers ships `MarginMSELoss` for this setup.

Typical production shape: a hybrid or distilled bi-encoder first stage, a small cross-encoder over the top 50 to 200, and the final few results sent to the user or an LLM. Measure accuracy and p99 latency at several k values on your own queries before fixing k.

blocks.question: Your budget for reranking is 60 ms per query on one GPU. With the model card's V100 numbers and the k / T model, which configuration fits?
options: MiniLM-L12-v2 over 100 candidates
MiniLM-L6-v2 over 100 candidates
BERT-large over 30 candidates
MiniLM-L6-v2 over 200 candidates
blocks.explain: MiniLM-L6-v2 needs 100 / 1800 s = 55.6 ms for 100 pairs. L12 needs 104.2 ms, BERT-large needs 300 ms for 30, and L6 over 200 needs 111 ms. Real overheads (tokenization, transfer) also count, so leave headroom.

blocks.question: Why does Margin-MSE train on the score difference instead of asking the student to reproduce the teacher's raw score?
options: Because the teacher's raw scores are not available after training
Because MSE cannot be computed on raw scores
Because the margin is always positive
Because different architectures produce scores on very different ranges, and ranking only depends on order and gaps
blocks.explain: The paper observed that cross-encoders, dot-product models and others have distinct score ranges. Matching margins lets the student keep its natural range while learning the teacher's preferences. The margin can even be negative when the teacher disagrees with the label.

blocks.question: A colleague proposes caching cross-encoder scores for every (query, document) pair to remove reranking latency. When does this actually help?
options: Only for repeated exact queries (head queries) over an unchanged candidate set; the long tail of new queries still pays full cost
Always, because cross-encoder scores never change
Never, because the scores depend on batch size
Only if the model uses sigmoid outputs
blocks.explain: A score is a function of the exact query and document text. Caching works for frequent repeated queries, which Hofstatter et al. also note as the exception, but most queries in real traffic are unique and must be scored live.
